strengths: Presents a well-motivated and technically rigorous generalization of Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms (EDAs) to leverage known decomposability of the objective function via a junction-tree formulation, complete with a clean generalization of classical max-plus message passing to distributional value functions.

Provides multiple, complementary derivations of the method (direct message-passing derivation in the main text/Sec. A.4, and an independent maximum-entropy/probabilistic-graphical-model derivation in Sec. A.5), lending credibility and generality to the core algorithmic idea.

Extensive empirical evaluation: synthetic functions with controlled decomposition across varying sequence length (L up to 400) and alphabet size (D up to 100), plus four real protein property-prediction landscapes (AAV, Amyloid, Gcn4, TDP-43) derived from AlphaFold3 structures, with statistically significant improvements over baselines (paired t-tests, 20 seeds, confidence intervals).
Good set of baselines within the EDA family (naive EDA, FDA, PPO-style update) that isolate the contribution of factorized search distributions versus message-passing value functions.

Thorough robustness and ablation studies (Sec. A.9): effect of contact threshold on decomposability/accuracy trade-off, random graph mutation robustness, runtime comparisons, and behavior on less-decomposable proteins (GB1, ynzC, CreiLOV), which honestly reports cases where the method's advantage shrinks.
Detailed reproducibility documentation (architectures, hyperparameter sweeps, dataset sources, training details) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The method fundamentally depends on a known or inferable decomposition (junction tree); the only concrete mechanism shown for obtaining this in a real domain is an AlphaFold3-contact-thresholding heuristic for proteins, which is somewhat ad hoc and not validated in any other scientific design domain (circuits, materials, telescopes) mentioned as motivating examples.

Empirical comparisons are limited to baselines within the same EDA/policy-optimization lineage (naive EDA, FDA, PPO-style update); no comparison to other widely used generative/model-based design approaches referenced in related work (e.g., CbAS, autofocused oracles, Bayesian optimization with additive structure) that could contextualize DADO's benefit relative to the broader design literature.

On less-decomposable real proteins (GB1, ynzC, CreiLOV, relegated to the appendix) DADO's advantage over FDA and even the naive EDA diminishes or disappears, indicating the method's benefits are contingent on favorable decomposition structure that may not hold broadly, somewhat undercutting the generality of the main claims.

The paper explicitly sets aside the accuracy of the learned property predictor f(x) as out of scope, yet real-world utility of the discovered high-scoring designs depends critically on this accuracy; no wet-lab or independent-oracle validation is provided to confirm that optimized designs are truly higher quality rather than exploiting predictor artifacts.

The reproducibility section states code is available on GitHub but the actual repository link is missing/blank in the provided manuscript, undermining verification of the reproducibility claim as presented.

The exposition is dense and heavily notation-laden (multiple redundant derivations across main text and appendix), which may hinder accessibility for readers less familiar with message passing and EDA/RL formalisms.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: leveraging known/learned decomposability of discrete objective functions for more sample-efficient distributional optimization (EDA/policy optimization), a genuinely underexplored angle relative to prior work focused on inaccurate oracles.

Solid theoretical development: the paper carefully derives DADO from classical message-passing for exact optimization, generalizes to distributional value functions with a clear lower-bound justification, and additionally provides an independent max-entropy/soft-Q derivation (Sec. A.4) that arrives at a structurally similar algorithm, lending credibility and generality to the approach.

Good positioning relative to related work, clearly distinguishing DADO from FDA, Bayesian-network EDAs (Pelikan), chain-structured RL policy optimization, and additive-model Bayesian optimization, explaining why none of these can handle general junction-tree-structured coordination via message-passing.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical validation: synthetic landscapes at multiple sequence lengths (up to L=200) with controlled reciprocal sign epistasis, plus real protein property predictors (4+3 datasets) built from AlphaFold3 structural contact graphs, showing consistent (though not universal) improvements over a naive EDA.

Useful ablations: sample-budget (K) sweeps and a case study varying the contact-distance threshold t that shows a clear, interpretable tradeoff between decomposition strength, predictive accuracy, and optimization speed (GB1 case).
Reproducibility is supported by detailed hyperparameter sweep description and public code release.
weaknesses: The primary empirical baseline throughout is only a decomposition-unaware ('naive') EDA; despite explicitly discussing FDA and Bayesian-network-based EDAs as closest related work, no direct empirical comparison to these decomposition-aware alternatives is provided, making it hard to isolate the specific benefit of the message-passing/value-function coordination mechanism versus simpler factorization schemes.

The method assumes the junction tree decomposition is given or can be reliably constructed a priori (e.g., via AlphaFold3 contact thresholding); the sensitivity of results to decomposition misspecification is only lightly explored (one threshold sweep on GB1), and the harder problem of learning/discovering decompositions from data is left entirely to future work despite being central to real-world applicability.

Mixed and inconsistently explained results: TDP-43 shows no significant benefit, and the explanation offered (many near-optimal local optima) is speculative and not empirically substantiated; the Gcn4 case (poor decomposition due to intrinsic disorder) is included but its implications for practical deployment of the method are not deeply analyzed.

Search distributions are limited to simple MLP-based autoregressive factors; no exploration of more expressive generative models (e.g., VAEs, diffusion) is conducted despite these being highlighted as a key motivating advantage of the distributional optimization framing.

Evaluation remains purely in silico with learned/synthetic surrogate objectives rather than any real-world or wet-lab validation, limiting evidence of practical impact for the motivating scientific design applications (protein engineering, circuit design, telescope design) mentioned in the introduction.

The paper explicitly scopes out entropy regularization, priors, and conditioning (features central to practical AI-guided design pipelines like CbAS), which somewhat limits the demonstrated relevance to realistic design workflows despite claims about extensibility.
